title: Must and need
intro: This unit is about obligation and need: *Gitmeliyim* (I must go), *Bana su lazım* (I need water), *Gitmem lazım* (I need to go), *Gitmek zorundayım* (I have to go). It ends with a second use of `-mAlI`, the confident guess: *Evde olmalı* (She must be at home).

blocks.text: The necessitative (*gereklilik kipi*) is the stem + `-mAlI` + the type I endings: *git-* + *-meli* + *-y-* + *-im* → *gitmeliyim* (I must go, I should go). It covers both a duty and a piece of advice: *Doktora gitmelisin* (You should see a doctor).

blocks.label: Necessitative
lines: -malı   after a, ı, o, u   yapmalı, okumalı
-meli   after e, i, ö, ü   gelmeli, gitmeli

blocks.text: The two vowels of the suffix go together: *-malı* or *-meli*. The stem never changes, because `-mAlI` starts with a consonant: *gitmeli*, *etmeli*, *demeli*, *yemeli*. A buffer y comes in before the endings for **I** and **we**: *gitmeliyim*, *gitmeliyiz*.

rows.en: he, she or it must go

blocks.text: **Negative.** Put `-mA` before `-mAlI`: *gitmemeliyim* (I mustn't go, I shouldn't go), *yapmamalısın* (you shouldn't do it).

**Questions.** The ending moves onto `mI`, as with every type I tense: *Gitmeli miyim?* (Should I go?). With a question word there is no `mI`: *Ne yapmalıyım?* (What should I do?). For **they**, *-lAr* stays on the verb: *Gitmeliler mi?*

items.en: You have a fever, you should see a doctor.

items.tr: Bu ilacı günde üç kere almalısınız.
items.seg: Bu ilacı günde üç kere al|malı|sınız.
items.en: You must take this medicine three times a day.
You should drink a lot of water.
You shouldn't smoke.
What should I do?
What time should we come?

blocks.text: Don't forget the buffer: *gitmeliyim*, not *gitmelim*. And the negative is one word, with `-mA` inside: *gitmemeliyim*, not *gitmeli değilim*.

English has **must**, **have to** and **should**; Turkish `-mAlI` covers **must** and **should**, and the tone of voice decides how strong it is. French devoir works the same way: tu dois partir, *gitmelisin*.

sections.title: Bana su lazım: need with lazım and gerek

blocks.text: *Lazım* (necessary, needed) and *gerek* (need; necessary) are not verbs. They come at the end of the sentence, and the person who needs something goes into the dative ([A1 unit 7](gp-dative)): *Bana su lazım* (I need water: literally **to me water is necessary**). Both are everyday words; *gerek* sounds a little more formal.

**With an infinitive**, *lazım* and *gerek* state a general need without saying who has it: *Erken kalkmak lazım* (One has to get up early; we have to get up early), *Bilet almak gerek* (We need to buy tickets). The verb *gerekmek* (to be necessary) does the same: *Bilet almak gerekiyor*.

**For a person**, Turkish uses a set pattern: the stem + `-mA` + a possessive ending ([A1 unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes)) + *lazım* or *gerek*: *gitmem lazım* (I need to go: literally **my going is necessary**). Learn it as a pattern for now: this `-mA` makes a verbal noun, which [B1 unit 4](gp-ma-possessive) explains in full.

rows.en: he or she needs to go

blocks.text: The `-mA` follows two-way harmony and the possessive four-way harmony after it: *yapmam, yapman, yapması, yapmamız, yapmanız, yapmaları lazım*. A question puts `mI` after *lazım*: *Gitmem lazım mı?* (Do I need to go?)

**A third way.** You can also say **need** with the noun *ihtiyaç* (need), a possessive and *var*, like *Arabam var* ([A1 unit 9](gp-possessive-have)); the thing needed goes into the dative: *Yardıma ihtiyacım var* (I need help). Note the softening of ç to c: *ihtiyacım*, *ihtiyacın*.

items.en: Ali needs a doctor.
I need to go to the pharmacy.
We need to get up early tomorrow.
Do we need to buy tickets?
You need to make an appointment.
Do you need help?

blocks.text: *Gitmem lazım* (I need to go) and *gitmem* on its own (I don't go, the negative aorist of [unit 4](gp-aorist-negative)) are spelled the same. *Lazım* or *gerek* after the verb tells you which one you have.
*Lazım* takes no personal ending: *Bana su lazım*, not *Ben su lazımım*. The person goes into the dative.
*Gerek yok, teşekkürler* (No need, thanks) is a polite way to turn down help or an extra effort.

**Have to** is the infinitive + *zorunda* (literally **in its necessity**) + the endings of **to be**: *Gitmek zorundayım* (I have to go). It stresses an obligation from outside: a rule, a timetable, a situation you can't change.

rows.en: he or she has to go

blocks.text: **Past and future** come from the copula or from *kalmak*, to remain: *gitmek zorundaydım* (I had to go: it was required, [unit 2](gp-past-copula)), *gitmek zorunda kaldım* (I had to go: I was forced to, I had no choice), *gitmek zorunda kalacağım* (I'll have to go).

head: Turkish
English
rows: I had to go (it was required).
I had to go (I was forced to).

blocks.text: **Don't have to** is *zorunda değil*: *Gelmek zorunda değilsin* (You don't have to come). It is not the same as **mustn't**, *gelmemelisin*: the first leaves you free, the second tells you not to.

blocks.caption: Four ways to talk about coming
head: Turkish
English
rows: You must come. You should come.
You mustn't come. You shouldn't come.

blocks.text: **Rules and signs** use the infinitive with *yasak* (forbidden) or *zorunlu* (compulsory), often with the formal `-DIr` of [A1 unit 3](gp-copula-present): *Burada sigara içmek yasaktır* (Smoking is forbidden here), *Kask takmak zorunludur* (Wearing a helmet is compulsory).

items.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You have to wear a seat belt in the car.

items.tr: Otobüs gelmedi, taksiye binmek zorunda kaldık.
items.seg: Otobüs gelmedi, taksiye bin|mek zorunda kal|dı|k.
items.en: The bus didn't come, so we had to take a taxi.
I don't have to work this evening.
Parking is forbidden here.

blocks.text: The ending goes on *zorunda* and follows its back a, whatever the verb: *gitmek zorundayım*, not *zorundayim*; *gelmek zorundasınız*.
English **mustn't** and **don't have to** are as different as Turkish *gelmemelisin* and *gelmek zorunda değilsin*. French draws the same line: tu ne dois pas venir, tu n'es pas obligé de venir.
Like English **must**, `-mAlI` also says what you think is almost certainly true: *Ayşe evde olmalı* (Ayşe must be at home: her car is outside).

With nouns, adjectives, numbers and places, add *olmalı*, from *olmak*: *Yorgun olmalısın* (You must be tired), *Saat beş olmalı* (It must be five o'clock), *Bu çanta Elif'in olmalı* (This bag must be Elif's). With an action verb, the guess is usually about what you expect to happen: *Tren birazdan gelmeli* (The train should be here soon).

items.en: The lights are on: they must be at home.
You must be very tired.
It must be ten o'clock.
This bag must be Elif's.
The train should be here soon.

blocks.text: **How sure are you?** *Galiba evde* and *Herhâlde evde* (She's probably at home) are softer guesses; *Evde olmalı* is surer; *Evde olabilir* ([unit 5](gp-abil-uses)) only says it's possible.
For a guess about a state, *olmalı* goes after the adjective: *Aç olmalısın* (You must be hungry). *Açmalısın*, without *ol-*, means **you must open**.
A guess about the past, **she must have left**, needs a form you will meet later ([C1 unit 1](gp-mis-olmali)). For now, say it with *galiba*: *Galiba gitti* (I think she's left).

summary: **Must, should**: stem + `-mAlI` + type I ending: *gitmeliyim, gitmelisin, gitmeli*. Negative *gitmemeliyim*; question *Gitmeli miyim?*
**Need**: the person in the dative + noun + *lazım* or *gerek*: *Bana su lazım*. Or *ihtiyaç*: *Yardıma ihtiyacım var*.
**Need to**: *-mAk lazım* for everyone (*Erken kalkmak lazım*), and the set pattern *gitmem, gitmen, gitmesi lazım* for a person.
*Gitmem lazım* (I need to go) and *gitmem* (I don't go) look the same: *lazım* tells them apart.
**Have to**: *-mAk zorundayım*; **had to** *zorundaydım* or *zorunda kaldım*; **don't have to** *zorunda değilim*, not the same as *-mAmAlI*, **mustn't**.
A confident guess: *Evde olmalı*, *Yorgun olmalısın*, *Saat beş olmalı*.
